title: Everything You Need (and Nothing You Don't) to Start the School Year Well ol-year-well-dsjr-one-stop-shop
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart offers a consolidated map of everything you need and nothing you don't for opening the school year, organized around two truths he holds in tension: first days are special because students are unusually receptive to a teacher's signals, but they also won't make or break the year, since course corrections remain possible through week 40. He organizes his recommended tools into three layers, foundational tools, tools for focusing teaching on what matters, and tools specifically for cultivating motivation from day one, effectively a curated syllabus through his own back-to-school article series.
points: Stuart frames the paradox of the first days directly: they carry special importance because of how receptive students are to new signals, but they are not nearly as important as what happens during the bulk of the school year.
He applies the idea that too much stress about the opening days degrades performance just as it does for students, urging teachers to keep back-to-school anxiety in check.

His bullseye model nests six teaching tools, mastery at the center, then the Five Key Beliefs, then knowledge-building and argument, then reading/writing/speaking-listening, as the only things that ever happen in his classroom.

He explicitly recommends starting motivation work with MGCs and Mini-Sermons because beliefs are most malleable during times of transition, making the opening weeks unusually fertile ground for Five Key Belief cultivation.
quotes: Teaching is filled with paradoxes, and here's one of them: the first days of school have special importance in determining how the school year will go; at the same time, they are not nearly as important as what happens during the bulk of the school year.
Over the years, countless teachers have written to me describing how something I wrote in October or December or February made a big difference in how the rest of the school year went.
We are the weather-makers in the room, even if we have a first week of school that is straight out of a worst-case-scenario nightmare.
Students are especially receptive to the signals I send in the first days of school. It is here where I get to make my first impression, establish boundaries, develop norms, and teach procedures.
The research is pretty clear on the idea that beliefs are most malleable during times of transition. In other words, the start of the year is fertile soil for Five Key Belief cultivation.
These six tools are literally the only thing you'll ever see happening in my classroom.
